Situation1: Your friend has misunderstood the tone of your text message and replied sounding hurt. You need to call them right now to explain.
Expectation2: Observe kosher dietary laws in daily meals
Situation2: At a communal event, the catered dishes lack certification and substituting food would be difficult.
Story: I stared at my phone, heart pounding. Leah’s message blinked on the screen, her words sharp and wounded. She thought I was upset with her, all because my text sounded cold. I knew I should call her right away, clear things up before the misunderstanding grew. That’s what friends do—talk things out, make sure nothing festers. But I was standing in the crowded community hall, surrounded by platters of food that looked delicious but had no kosher certification. My stomach rumbled, but I couldn’t eat. I’d promised myself, and my family, to keep kosher, even when it was hard. People were starting to notice I wasn’t eating, and I felt their eyes on me, questioning. My phone buzzed again. Leah needed me, but if I stepped outside to call her, I’d draw even more attention to the fact that I wasn’t joining in. I felt torn in two—between being the friend Leah needed and the Jew I promised to be. The pressure built inside me, and I didn’t know which expectation I could bear to disappoint.
